meta.title: Who really said "Hello, Clarice"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Lecter never says “Hello, Clarice” in The Silence of the Lambs. The line is “Good evening, Clarice.” The misquote is real — but only in the 2001 sequel.
meta.ogDescription: “Hello, Clarice” appears nowhere in The Silence of the Lambs. Ted Tally’s line is “Good evening, Clarice.” Lecter says the famous version in Hannibal (2001).

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “Good evening, Clarice.”
answer.authorDates: b. 9 April 1952 · Screenwriter of the 1991 film
answer.sourceLine: In the finished film Hannibal Lecter greets Clarice Starling exactly once by name, through the bars of a Memphis holding cage: “Good evening, Clarice.” The word “hello” is not spoken anywhere in The Silence of the Lambs. The popular version is not invented, though — it belongs to the sequel, where Lecter answers a phone with “Well, hello Clarice.”

source.excerpt:
Hannibal Lecter: [reading a book] Good evening, Clarice.
Clarice Starling: I thought you might like your drawings back, Doctor. Just until you get your view.
trail: Wikiquote’s transcription of the film ↗ contains exactly one greeting from Lecter to Starling — “Good evening, Clarice” — and the word “hello” does not appear anywhere on the page. The raw wikitext was searched directly rather than read in summary.

Wikiquote’s Misquotations ↗ page carries a dedicated entry: the line “was never once used in the film itself,” though Lecter “does at one point utter a similar phrase of ‘Good evening, Clarice.’” Quote Investigator has no article on this phrase, so this entry is the anchor here.

The phrase is real, but it is the sequel’s. Wikiquote’s transcription of Hannibal (2001) ↗ has Lecter answering a phone: “Is this Clarice? Well, hello Clarice.” That screenplay is credited to David Mamet and Steven Zaillian.
A parody vector predates the sequel by five years: in The Cable Guy (1996) ↗, Jim Carrey’s Chip imitates Lecter and says “Hello, Clarice. It’s good to see you again.”
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the finished film at Wikiquote ↗. Note that the undated screenplay draft published at IMSDb renders this same greeting as “Good afternoon, Clarice” — see the note below.

Screen writing is work-for-hire, so the rights sit with the film’s producer/distributor rather than with Ted Tally personally — Orion Pictures released the film, and Orion’s library is now owned by Amazon MGM Studios ↗. The single line is quoted here for identification and fact-checking.

author.name: Ted Tally
author.heading: Who actually wrote the line
author.metaLine: b. 9 April 1952 · American playwright and screenwriter
author.bio: William Theodore “Ted” Tally is an American playwright and screenwriter who came to film from the theatre, where he won an Obie Award for his play Terra Nova. His adaptation of Thomas Harris’s The Silence of the Lambs won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay at the 64th Academy Awards, along with a Writers Guild of America Award and an Edgar from the Mystery Writers of America. He returned to the Lecter material a decade later, adapting Red Dragon (2002); his other credits include White Palace, All the Pretty Horses and 12 Strong.

misattribution.heading: Where it goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The error here is not who — it is what. Nobody is falsely credited: the film is real, the character is right, the actor is right. Only the words drifted, and then drifted into a different film.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Misquotations ↗ entry states the line “was never once used in the film itself,” and that Lecter “does at one point utter a similar phrase of ‘Good evening, Clarice.’” Searching the full transcription ↗ returns no instance of “hello” at all.

The phrase exists — in the sequel. In Hannibal (2001) ↗, Lecter picks up Inspector Pazzi’s phone and says “Is this Clarice? Well, hello Clarice.” That screenplay is by David Mamet and Steven Zaillian, not Ted Tally, and it arrived a decade after the line people are quoting.

Hopkins performed the line; Lecter is a fictional character. Neither wrote it. The screenplay credit for The Silence of the Lambs is Ted Tally’s ↗ alone, and it won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay at the 64th Academy Awards.

misattribution.truthLine: The line people mean is “Good evening, Clarice” — from Ted Tally’s screenplay for The Silence of the Lambs (1991), transcribed here ↗. The line people say is “Well, hello Clarice” — and Lecter does not get around to saying it until 2001.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: “Hello, Clarice” is among the most quoted lines in American cinema, and it is missing from the film everyone quotes it from. Search a full transcription of The Silence of the Lambs and the word “hello” does not turn up once. What Lecter actually says, reading a book in a Memphis holding cage in his last face-to-face scene with Starling, is “Good evening, Clarice.”

What makes this misquote unusual is that it is not a fabrication — it is a filing error. The line is real; it is simply in the wrong film and the wrong decade. Parodists were already saying it by 1996, when Jim Carrey’s cable installer drops into a Lecter impression in The Cable Guy. Five years later the franchise itself said it out loud: in Hannibal, Lecter answers a dying man’s phone with “Is this Clarice? Well, hello Clarice.” Whether Mamet and Zaillian were winking at the misquote is not documented anywhere this page could verify. The effect was the same either way.
context.detailsSummary: Two things this page cannot tell you
detailsBody: Whether the greeting is Harris’s or Tally’s. The film is adapted from Thomas Harris’s 1988 novel, and the Memphis cage scene exists in the book. Whether Harris wrote a greeting into it — and in what words — could not be checked: every scanned copy of the novel is lending-restricted, and full-text search inside them is gated. This page therefore credits the film’s credited screenwriter and makes no claim about the novel in either direction. Crediting a film with a line it inherited from its source book is a real and common error; it simply could not be ruled in or out here.

Who chose the word “evening.” The undated draft of Tally’s screenplay published at IMSDb ↗ reads “Good afternoon, Clarice,” and it differs from the finished film elsewhere in the same scene, so it is plainly an earlier version rather than the shooting script. Whether “evening” came from a later revision by Tally, from Jonathan Demme on the day, or from Hopkins himself is not something the available sources settle. Tally remains the film’s sole credited screenwriter.
context.pull: “Hello, Clarice” is not a memory of nothing. It is a memory of the sequel, filed under the original.
